question: What is the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking?

facts.text: Optimistic locking adds a version column, updates only if the version is unchanged, and retries on conflict.
Pessimistic locking locks the row with SELECT FOR UPDATE, so other transactions wait.

answer: Optimistic locking keeps a version column and only applies an update if the version is still the one you read, retrying if someone else changed it. Pessimistic locking takes a lock up front with SELECT FOR UPDATE so other transactions have to wait.

question: How do ETag and If-None-Match enable conditional requests?

facts.text: The server sends an ETag header identifying the current version of the resource.
The client sends the stored ETag back in an If-None-Match header on later requests.
If the resource is unchanged the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body, so the client reuses its cache.

answer: The server includes an ETag header that identifies the version of the resource. On the next request the client sends that ETag in If-None-Match. If nothing changed, the server answers 304 Not Modified without a body and the client reuses what it cached.

question: Why does a CPU-heavy synchronous function block a Node.js server?

facts.text: Node runs JavaScript on a single main thread driven by the event loop.
A synchronous function holds that thread until it returns, so the event loop cannot process other callbacks or requests.
Heavy work should move to worker threads or a separate process.

answer: Node executes your JavaScript on one main thread that the event loop drives. A synchronous function keeps that thread busy until it returns, so the event loop cannot run any other callbacks or handle other requests meanwhile. CPU-heavy work belongs in worker threads or another process.

question: What does the GIL do in CPython?

facts.text: The GIL is a mutex that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time in a CPython process.
It therefore prevents CPU-bound Python threads from running in parallel on multiple cores.
I/O-bound threads still benefit because the GIL is released while waiting on I/O.

answer: The GIL is a mutex so only one thread runs Python bytecode at any moment in a CPython process. That means CPU-bound threads cannot run in parallel on several cores. I/O-bound threads still help because the GIL is released while they wait for I/O.
